summary: Mission Dhruva, created by Anthahkarana, is an English–Kannada science adventure for children aged 7–12. Players care for a fictional Mars outpost by sharing limited energy, growing food, repairing a recycling system and preparing for a storm. Through predictions, experiments and visible consequences, children discover how connected systems sustain life—and apply that thinking back on Earth.
details:
Mission Dhruva turns space exploration into a learning experience built around a simple cycle: predict, experiment, observe and reflect.

Players take responsibility for an outpost in Jezero Crater on Mars. They distribute a fixed energy budget between essential systems, investigate how water and light affect crops, reconnect a water recycling loop and prepare shelter supplies. These activities influence a three-wave storm challenge, where players weigh competing priorities and see the consequences of their decisions.

The game’s central lesson is that living systems are interconnected. Giving one system more energy leaves less for another. Extra water cannot replace missing light. Preparation changes what happens during an emergency. A final reflection connects these discoveries to an everyday situation on Earth, followed by a personalized mission certificate.

Our intended impact is to make scientific reasoning approachable for young learners, including Kannada-speaking children. The experience supports English and Kannada, optional narration, mobile layouts and untimed decisions. Children can read and reason at their own pace without needing an account or specialized hardware.

We developed the project using Next.js, React, TypeScript, Zustand and CSS. Sarvam AI provides Dhruva’s narration and the demonstration film’s voiceover; existing Chinnu character narration uses ElevenLabs. AI-generated artwork creates the fictional Mars environments. The demonstration film combines actual application captures, narration, titles and captions using FFmpeg.

The creative element is the connection between preparation, experimentation and consequences. The player’s earlier decisions carry into later challenges, making science part of the gameplay.

We considered reading load, language access, limited resources, feedback after mistakes and scientific transparency. NASA resources inform the setting and hazards, while weather values, crop requirements and resource effects are explicitly simplified teaching models. The project does not claim to reproduce NASA measurements or provide an engineering simulation.
